paragraphs.source_en: “Well, after so long, merely getting a look around Tokyo is worth the trip. Kushami! My uncle here has come all the way from Shizuoka to Tokyo because the Red Cross general meeting is being held this time. Today I took him to Ueno Park, and we have just come back from looking around; that is why he is wearing the full formal coat I ordered for him at Shirokiya.” Meitei said this deliberately to draw the master’s attention to it. When the master looked, sure enough, the old man was wearing a frock coat. He was indeed wearing the frock coat, but it did not fit him in the least. The sleeves were too long, the collar gaped open, a hollow formed across the back, and the armpits were hoisted up; even if one set out to make it ill-shaped, one could hardly deform it with such elaborate care. Moreover, his white shirt and white detachable collar had separated from each other, so that when he tilted his head back his Adam’s apple showed between them. Most remarkable of all, it was impossible to tell whether his black necktie belonged to the collar or to the shirt. The frock coat could still be endured, but the white topknot he wore on his head was truly a spectacle. I looked closely again at his celebrated iron fan; it lay neatly beside his knees. By this time the master had gradually recovered his composure, and, applying the full fruits of his spiritual discipline to the observation of the old man’s dress, he could not help being somewhat astonished. Previously he had not quite believed Meitei’s tales, supposing that his uncle could hardly be as Meitei described; but now, meeting him, he found that the reality exceeded the report. If his own pockmarks could serve as material for historical research, then this old man’s topknot and iron fan surely possessed even greater value. The master very much wanted to ask about the origin of the fan, but could hardly put such a blunt question; yet feeling it would be rude to let the conversation lapse, he asked a perfectly ordinary question:
